title: Commenting on problematic situations
subtitle: in a fix, take the bull by the horns, the tide has turned
summary: Learn the nouns, verbs and idioms English uses to describe difficult situations, to talk about dealing with them and to say that things are finally changing.

lesson.heading: Types of problems and difficulties
lesson.text: English has a lot of different words for trouble. **Chaos** is total confusion, with no order at all. A **disaster** is an event that causes great harm or damage. If you are **in a dilemma** or **face a dilemma**, you must make a difficult choice between two things.

examples.text: The earthquake was a dreadful **disaster** for the country.
The transport system was in **chaos** for some time afterwards.
The government were faced with a **dilemma**: start reconstruction work at once or wait until the likelihood of aftershocks had passed.

lesson.heading: Being in trouble
rows: to be in a difficult situation
to be in a tight corner
to be in a situation that is hard to get out of
a problem seen positively - it needs great mental or physical effort and so tests your ability
lesson.note: The word challenge puts a positive slant on a problem: it focuses on the effort needed rather than on the trouble.

lesson.heading: Specific difficulties
lesson.text: You can be badly **affected** by all sorts of things, from the mildly **irritating** to the intensely **annoying**. Note that *irritating* means slightly annoying, while *annoying* is stronger.

examples.note: disrupt = prevent something from continuing as intended
collapse = fail because of a lack of support

examples.text: You can be **deprived of** something you value.
examples.note: deprive = have something taken away from you

examples.text: Your life may **lack** something that you would like.

lesson.heading: The related nouns
rows: effect (She had a profound effect on me.)
lesson.note: Remember: the verb is affect, the noun is effect.

lesson.heading: Idioms about dealing with problems
rows: not to do anything; let others act instead
to take the bull by the horns
act positively to face and attack the problem
do or say things that make the situation worse
to pour oil on troubled waters
do or say things that calm the situation down
to lay your cards on the table
state exactly what your position is

lesson.heading: More idioms for tackling a problem
lesson.text: Several idioms describe the effort of understanding a problem or making other people take it seriously.

examples.text: I **can't face** (the thought of) clearing up all this mess today.
examples.note: can't face = don't want to deal with

examples.text: We need a proper investigation to **get to the bottom of** things.
It's quite difficult to get people to **sit up and take notice**.
I'm trying to **get a grasp of** what's happening; it's not easy.

lesson.heading: Idioms about changes in problem situations
lesson.text: When a bad situation starts to improve - or stops dead - English reaches for idioms.

examples.text: **The tide has turned** for us; better days are ahead.
We can see **the light at the end of the tunnel** at last.
examples.note: see that a difficult situation may be ending soon

examples.text: I'm afraid we've just **come to a dead end** with our plans.
I think I've reached a **turning point** in my career.
The government and the unions have **buried the hatchet** for the time being.
examples.note: made peace, stopped fighting each other

examples.text: All that trouble last year was just **swept under the carpet** in the end.
examples.note: ignored or deliberately forgotten, without solving it

lesson.text: Learn these idioms with their prepositions - *lay your cards on the table*, *pour oil on troubled waters*, *get to the bottom of things* - because the preposition is the part learners most often get wrong.

exercises.prompt: After the earthquake, city transport was in ___.
exercises.explanation: Chaos is a state of total confusion, where there is no order at all.

exercises.prompt: Should I take the job in New York or the one in Sydney? It's quite a ___.
exercises.explanation: A dilemma is a situation where you have to make a difficult decision between two things.

exercises.prompt: Can you help Grandpa fill out that form? It's so long and complicated that he's getting in a bit of a ___.
exercises.explanation: To be in a muddle means to be confused or mixed up.

exercises.prompt: The manager told his staff that he didn't want to hear the word 'problems', but rather they should talk about ___.
exercises.explanation: Challenge presents a problem positively: it tests your ability rather than simply defeating you.

exercises.prompt: I wonder if you could help me out - I'm in a bit of a tight ___.
exercises.explanation: To be in a tight corner means to be in a situation that is hard to get out of.

exercises.prompt: The floods are the worst natural ___ the country has experienced this century.
exercises.explanation: A disaster is an event which causes great harm or damage.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence beginning with the phrase that completes it.

pairs.left: Ben decided he would immediately lay his cards
The best thing to do is just to take the bull
Fortunately we can now see the light at the end
It'll take ages before we can get to the bottom
It's asking for trouble to sweep things
You can always rely on Naomi to pour oil

exercises.prompt: Match the beginnings with their endings.

pairs.left: At the moment my research seems to have come
Claire has now reached a turning point
The unions and the government have buried
Selim feels at last that the tide

exercises.prompt: No, please, don't say anything: you'll only ___.
exercises.explanation: To stir things up means to do or say things that make a situation worse.

exercises.prompt: You've been messing around achieving nothing for too long; it's time you ___!
exercises.explanation: To get your act together means to organise yourself so that you can respond properly.

exercises.prompt: At last I've managed to get him to ___; he's paid no attention at all to us so far.
exercises.explanation: To get someone to sit up and take notice means to make them pay attention.

exercises.statement: Paula was profoundly affected by her meeting with Angus, so we can also say: Paula's meeting with Angus had a profound affect on her.
exercises.explanation: The noun is effect: Paula's meeting with Angus had a profound effect on her.
